theme: The woman and the dragon; the two beasts
readingInstruction: Read Revelation 12:1-13:18. This is among the most symbolic parts of the book. Read it as a drama in three parts: the woman and the dragon, the war in heaven, and the two beasts who serve the dragon. Notice the repeated pattern of the dragon’s power and the saints’ victory.
settingTheScene: After the seventh trumpet, the book moves to a second half, which looks at the spiritual conflict behind history. John is shown the “great sign” of a woman and a dragon, then the beasts. These are not simply events to come but pictures of realities that have been present since the fall: Satan’s enmity against the offspring of the woman (Genesis 3:15), the state’s tendency to demand worship (Daniel 3 and 7), and the false religion that serves it. For first-century Christians under Rome, the beast from the sea was plainly the empire and its emperors, and the beast from the land was the priesthood and propaganda of the imperial cult. For us, these chapters expose similar powers in every age, and may point to a final climax of their rebellion.
observation: “Behold, a great red dragon, with seven heads and ten horns” (12:3).
“One who is to rule all the nations with a rod of iron” (12:5).
“That ancient serpent, who is called the devil and Satan, the deceiver of the whole world” (12:9).
“They have conquered him by the blood of the Lamb and by the word of their testimony” (12:11).
“He knows that his time is short” (12:12).
“A beast rising out of the sea, with ten horns and seven heads” (13:1).
“The book of life of the Lamb who was slain” (13:8).
“Here is a call for the endurance and faith of the saints” (13:10).
interpretation:
A great sign appears in heaven: a woman clothed with the sun, with the moon under her feet and a crown of twelve stars, about to give birth. She represents the people of God, from whom the Messiah comes: Israel in the Old Testament, and the church in the New (some also see Mary as the model). A great red dragon stands before her, with seven heads, ten horns, and seven diadems, ready to devour her child. His tail sweeps down a third of the stars (fallen angels). The child is born, “a male child, one who is to rule all the nations with a rod of iron” (Psalm 2:9), and is caught up to God and to his throne. This compresses the life of Christ: his birth, his rule, and his ascension, with the cross implied. The woman flees into the wilderness, where she is nourished for 1,260 days.

Then war breaks out in heaven. Michael and his angels fight the dragon, and “the great dragon was thrown down, that ancient serpent, who is called the devil and Satan, the deceiver of the whole world.” He is identified fully: the serpent of Genesis 3, the accuser. A loud voice proclaims: “Now the salvation and the power and the kingdom of our God and the authority of his Christ have come, for the accuser of our brothers has been thrown down.” Many see this as the effect of Christ’s death and ascension, when Satan’s accusing power was broken. And the means of victory: “And they have conquered him by the blood of the Lamb and by the word of their testimony, for they loved not their lives even unto death.” The church wins not by force but by the blood of Christ, faithful witness, and willingness to die. But “woe to you, O earth and sea, for the devil has come down to you in great wrath, because he knows that his time is short!” A defeated enemy is the most dangerous; he turns to persecute the woman and the rest of her offspring, “those who keep the commandments of God and hold to the testimony of Jesus.”

Chapter 13 introduces the dragon’s two agents. The first beast rises out of the sea with ten horns, seven heads, and blasphemous names. It resembles Daniel’s four beasts combined. The dragon gives it his power and throne and great authority. One of its heads seems to have a mortal wound that is healed (a parody of the resurrection). The whole earth marvels and worships the dragon and the beast: “Who is like the beast, and who can fight against it?” This mocks the praise of God, “Who is like you, O LORD?” It is allowed for forty-two months to utter blasphemies and “to make war on the saints and to conquer them.” All will worship it, “everyone whose name has not been written before the foundation of the world in the book of life of the Lamb who was slain.” And in the middle comes a call for the saints: “Here is a call for the endurance and faith of the saints.”

The second beast rises out of the earth, with two horns like a lamb but speaking like a dragon. It exercises the authority of the first beast and makes the earth worship it, performing signs and deceiving the inhabitants. It orders an image of the beast and causes all to be marked on the right hand or forehead, “so that no one can buy or sell unless he has the mark, that is, the name of the beast or the number of its name.” It is a parody of the Spirit, as the first beast is a parody of Christ. The number is given: “This calls for wisdom: let the one who has understanding calculate the number of the beast, for it is the number of a man, and his number is 666.” Many early Christians understood this by the Hebrew letters as pointing to Nero Caesar; others see it as a symbol of human imperfection (falling short of seven, repeated three times); others as a future individual. In every approach, the lesson is the same: the world powers that demand ultimate loyalty are in the service of the dragon, but they are allowed only a limited time, and the Lamb’s book of life cannot be erased.
connection: Genesis 3:15 is the first promise of the woman’s offspring and the serpent. Isaiah 66:7-9 and Micah 5:2-3 mention the birth of the Messiah. Psalm 2:9 is quoted in 12:5. Daniel 7:2-8 describes four beasts rising from the sea. Daniel 3 tells of the demand to worship an image. Job 1-2 and Zechariah 3:1-2 show Satan as accuser. Romans 8:33-34 answers the accuser. Luke 10:18 and John 12:31 describe Satan’s fall and judgment. 2 Thessalonians 2:3-12 describes the man of lawlessness. 1 John 2:18 and 4:3 speak of antichrists. Matthew 24:24 mentions false signs. Exodus 15:11 and Psalm 35:10 ask, “Who is like you?”
application:
When you feel overwhelmed by evil, remember how the saints conquer: by the blood of the Lamb, the word of their testimony, and not loving their lives even unto death.

Examine where the world’s powers ask for your ultimate loyalty (nation, money, ideology, security). Choose one area where you need to worship only the Lamb.

Pray for Christians who are living under regimes that demand allegiance contrary to Christ.
prayerPrompts: Thank Jesus for being the child who rules the nations.
Thank him that the accuser is conquered by his blood.
Ask him for courage to speak your testimony.
